The book cost me two coins at the Saturday stall, and I bought it for the cover, which was the green of old bottles. On the train home a folded sheet slid from between pages ninety and ninety-one. It was a letter, written in a hand that leaned forward as if hurrying to catch something.

'Dear Tomas,' it began. 'You will say I have chosen the wrong book again. I have. I always choose the books I would like you to read rather than the ones you would. But read the chapter about the lighthouse keeper, and then tell me you were bored. Your grandfather pretended to be bored by it for forty years and still knew it by heart.'

There followed a list of instructions for watering a lemon tree, and a line crossed out so firmly that the pen had torn the paper. At the bottom she had written: 'Come at Easter if your exams allow. If they do not, come anyway, and bring the exams.'

I do not know whether Tomas came at Easter. I do not know whether he read the chapter, or whether he sold the book without ever opening it, which would explain why the letter was still inside. I read the lighthouse chapter that night. I was not bored. I have kept the letter in the book, at page ninety, in case its proper reader ever goes looking for it.

items.stimulus:

Speaker 2 (Dov Achterberg, essayist): 'Every joke needs a target. Laughter is how a group reminds an outsider that he is outside; the warmth inside the circle is paid for by the cold beyond it.'

Speaker 3 (Ruth Okafor-Lind, physician): 'I have watched patients laugh at their own diagnoses. It changes nothing in the scans, yet it changes how they carry the news. Humour does not remove a burden; it alters its grip.'

items.stimulus: A student placed five identical shallow trays, each holding 500 g of water, in a closed room kept at 22 °C. items.stimulus:
Rome's aqueducts were not only feats of engineering; they were also problems of management. For much of the Republic, responsibility for the water supply was divided among elected officials who held office for short terms, which made steady, long-term maintenance difficult. Under Augustus this changed. A permanent board of water commissioners was created, and the trained slave workforce that the general Agrippa had kept for repairing the channels passed to the state after his death. Later emperors added further teams of labourers, plumbers and inspectors.

The most detailed account of the system comes from Sextus Julius Frontinus, who was appointed water commissioner in 97 CE. His treatise describes not only the routes and capacities of the aqueducts but also the abuses he found. Water-men accepted bribes to divert supplies; landowners along the routes tapped the channels illegally; and private users fitted pipes wider than their grants allowed. Frontinus compared the water actually flowing with the official records and reported that far more water entered the system than was recorded as being delivered.

Control rested on a few simple devices. A private user received water through a bronze nozzle of standard size, stamped and fixed in place, so that the permitted flow could in principle be checked. Grants of water were made to individuals, not to properties: when a holder died or sold the land, the right lapsed and had to be applied for again. Public fountains, baths and other public uses had priority over private grants.

Frontinus presented himself as a reformer, and his treatise is partly a record of his own diligence. Even so, it shows that the Roman state treated water as a public resource to be allocated, measured and policed, rather than as a commodity that anyone could simply take.
items.question: It can be inferred from the passage that making water grants personal rather than attached to property

options.text: was intended to raise the value of land along the aqueducts.
stopped landowners from tapping the channels illegally.
meant that public fountains received less water than before, since private users came first.
gave the authorities regular opportunities to review who was receiving water.

items.stimulus:
Most people tell small untruths every week. A friend asks whether we enjoyed the meal she cooked, and we say it was lovely; a colleague asks whether his presentation went well, and we assure him it did. These white lies are usually defended on the ground that they cost nothing and spare feelings. Strict moralists who condemn them can seem to value a rule above the person standing in front of them.

Yet the claim that white lies cost nothing deserves scrutiny. Praise works like a currency: its value depends on the belief that it is not handed out regardless of merit. If everyone knows that I call every meal lovely, my compliment tells my friend nothing, and on the day I genuinely admire her cooking I have no way of saying so that she can trust. The cost of a white lie is therefore not paid at the moment it is told, when it may indeed bring comfort, but later, and it is paid by every honest remark that follows.

There is a second cost. A colleague who is told that a weak presentation went well loses the chance to improve it. The lie protects his feelings today at the expense of his interests tomorrow, and it does so without asking him which he would prefer.

None of this means that every question deserves a blunt answer. Tact lies in choosing what to say and when, not in saying what is false. One may praise the effort, mention the one dish that worked, or simply say that the evening was a pleasure, which may be perfectly true. The kind response, in most cases, is a truthful one delivered with care.

items.stimulus:
Every morning we expect the sun to rise, bread to nourish us and dropped objects to fall. These expectations rest on past experience: we have observed such things many times and infer that they will continue. The eighteenth-century Scottish philosopher David Hume asked what entitles us to make that inference.

Hume noticed that any argument from observed cases to unobserved ones needs a hidden premise: that the future will resemble the past, or, more generally, that nature is uniform. The question is how this premise could be established. It cannot be proved by pure reasoning, as a theorem of geometry can, because there is no contradiction in imagining that bread might stop nourishing us tomorrow. A world in which the pattern breaks is strange, but it is perfectly conceivable.

Nor, Hume argued, can the premise be supported by experience. One might reply that the assumption of uniformity has always worked before. But to conclude from its past success that it will succeed in future is itself an inference from observed to unobserved cases - the very kind of inference whose credentials are in question. The defence therefore assumes what it is meant to prove.

Hume's conclusion was not that we should stop expecting the sun to rise. He held that we could not stop even if we tried. What carries us from past to future is not a chain of reasoning but custom: after repeated experience of one event following another, the mind simply comes to expect the second when it meets the first. Induction, on this view, is a deep and useful habit rather than a conclusion of reason.

Later philosophers have offered many responses. Some argue that the demand for a non-circular justification is unreasonable; others try to justify induction in terms of probability. None of these responses has won general agreement.
items.question: It can be inferred that, according to Hume as described in the passage, a person who has seen a thousand swans, all of them white,

options.text: has proved that all swans are white.
should stop expecting the next swan to be white.
is more certain than someone who has seen only ten swans, because after so many cases the inference has now become a deduction.
has no rational proof from these observations alone that the next swan will be white, but will naturally expect it to be.

items.explanation_ko: 1) 흄에 따르면 관찰한 사례에서 관찰하지 않은 사례로 가는 추론은 '자연은 한결같다'는 숨은 전제가 필요하고, 이 전제는 이성으로도 경험으로도 증명되지 않는다. 2) 그러나 반복 경험이 만든 습관(custom) 때문에 우리는 자연스럽게 다음 경우를 기대한다. 3) 따라서 D가 흄의 입장이다. 오답: A 관찰 횟수와 상관없이 증명은 되지 않는다. B 흄은 기대를 멈춰야 한다고 하지 않았고, 멈출 수도 없다고 보았다. C 관찰이 늘어도 귀납이 연역으로 바뀌지 않는다. 유형 팁: 철학 지문 추론에서는 '정당화되지 않는다'와 '그러니 믿지 말라'를 구분한다. → 정답 D

Assume that the sun's rays are parallel, so that any vertical object, its shadow and the ray passing over its top form right-angled triangles that are similar to the triangle formed by the post.
items.question: At that moment, a vertical flagpole on the same level ground casts a shadow 12 m long. How tall is the flagpole?

options.text: 6 m
9 m

items.explanation_ko: 1) 닮은 삼각형이므로 높이 : 그림자 = 1.5 : 2 = 0.75로 일정하다. 2) 깃대 높이 = 12 × 0.75 = 9 m. 어림 요령: 그림자가 6배(2 → 12)이므로 높이도 1.5 × 6 = 9 m. 오답: A 그림자를 2로 나누기만 했다. B 12에서 1.5를 뺐다(비율 대신 차이 사용). C 비를 뒤집어 12 × 2/1.5로 계산했다. D 12에 1.5를 곱했다. 유형 팁: 닮음 문제는 '같은 종류끼리'(높이:높이 = 그림자:그림자) 비를 세운다. → 정답 E

items.question: The council's claim depends on which one of the following assumptions?

Planting trees is the cheapest way of reducing temperatures in the district in summer.
Cooler pavements and shade outside will lead to lower temperatures inside nearby homes.

items.stimulus:
Every language has words for relatives, but languages divide up the family in strikingly different ways. English uses 'uncle' for a father's brother, a mother's brother and the husband of an aunt, and 'cousin' for any child of an aunt or uncle, whatever that child's sex and whichever parent links them. Latin, by contrast, had separate words for a father's brother and a mother's brother.

Some systems merge relatives even more widely. In what anthropologists call the Hawaiian type, a single term may cover one's father, father's brothers and mother's brothers, and one's siblings share a term with all of one's cousins of the same sex. In the Iroquois type, a father and a father's brother share a term, but a mother's brother has a different one. The children of a father's brother or of a mother's sister are called by sibling terms, while the children of a father's sister or of a mother's brother are called by separate 'cousin' terms.

Other languages draw distinctions that English ignores. Many languages of East and Southeast Asia distinguish older from younger siblings, and some choose the word according to the sex of the speaker as well as that of the sibling.

Such differences are not simply a matter of vocabulary. Kinship terms often track who lives together, who inherits from whom and whom one may marry. Where a father's brother shares the father's household and duties, calling him by the father's term may reflect a real social role. Yet the link is loose: a term can outlive the arrangements that produced it, and speakers whose language merges two relatives can still describe the difference between them when they need to.

items.stimulus:
The neat green lawn is one of the most expensive habits a city can have. Councils mow parks, verges and roundabouts many times a year, burning fuel and paying crews to keep grass at a height that serves no one but the mower. It is time to replace much of this turf with meadows of native wildflowers and grasses.

The ecological case is strong. A short lawn offers little to insects: one or two kinds of grass, cut before anything can flower. A meadow of native plants provides nectar and pollen across the seasons and shelter for the insects on which birds feed. Because native plants have grown alongside local insects for thousands of years, they tend to support far more species than ornamental imports.

Meadows also save money. Once established, they need cutting only once or twice a year, and they seldom need watering, even in dry summers, because deep-rooted native plants reach water that lawn grass cannot. The savings in fuel, labour and water could be spent on the parks themselves.

Some residents object that meadows look untidy. But tastes change. A century ago the clipped lawn was a luxury that signalled wealth; it became normal only because people grew used to it. In the town of Ellsby, where the council sowed a single roundabout with wildflowers last spring, the local paper received several letters of praise. Clearly, residents everywhere will welcome meadows once they see them.

Meadows are not right for every space. Sports pitches and picnic lawns must stay short, and paths should be mown through larger meadows so that people can still walk and play. But the default should change. Instead of asking why a patch of grass should be allowed to grow, councils should ask why it must be cut.
